articles.excerpt: Mariam al-Najar, a 24-year-old student from Khan Younis in Gaza, was waiting for a message that could change her life.When an email arrived two weeks after she applied for a scholarship from the University of Cassino and Southern Lazio in Italy, she felt, for a brief moment at least, that years of studying had finally paid off.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Is Israel’s Netanyahu preparing to fight Iran alone?list 2 of 3Eight countries denounce Israeli violations, attacks on healthcare in Gazalist 3 of 3Israel charges settler for killing Palestinian activist Awdah Hathaleenend of listThe university confirmed that she had been offered a place for a master’s degree in economics and management, one of the few times during a long period of despair that Mariam had felt any hope about the future.“Being accepted was like a ray of light that suddenly appeared and gave me a sense of life and hope again,” she told Al Jazeera. “I was applying for scholarships while feeling deeply hopeless and I never expected to receive an acceptance.”The scholarship offer was not just an opportunity for Mariam to continue higher studies at a leading university but also offered hope of a new future amid Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza.But securing a place at the university opened the door to a whole new set of challenges for Mariam.Italy was a main destination for the evacuation of Palestinian students from the Gaza Strip between 2025 and 2026.Approximately 229 students were evacuated from Gaza prior to May 2026, with another group of around 40 students joining in June 2026.Part of the reason for the high demand is attributed to the lower living and tuition costs in Italy compared to many other European countries.

articles.title: ‘No red line’: South Lebanon residents outraged as Israel resumes strikes
articles.excerpt: People in southern Lebanon question their government’s approach as Israel launches more attacks and displacement orders.As Israel resumes strikes and issues forced displacement orders in southern Lebanon, residents of the region are expressing anger and helplessness during ongoing talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials.For displaced families, the latest round of strikes on Thursday, which injured at least eight people, is further evidence that the June “ceasefire” has failed to protect them from Israeli military action. The Israeli military sparked the latest wave of panic by issuing a forced evacuation order for the town of al-Mansouri on Wednesday, marking its first displacement directive in weeks.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3WHO chief: Ebola outbreak in DRC spreading at ‘unprecedented rate’list 2 of 3Toronto police arrest two in US Consulate shooting investigationlist 3 of 3Trump signs new executive orders seeking to limit US birthright citizenshipend of list“Mansouri is not part of Israel’s occupation zone,” Yousef Shehemi, mayor of the neighbouring town of Majdal Zoun, told Al Jazeera’s Zeina Khodr. “But Israel has no red lines – they target where they want. They have not respected any ceasefire.”Families from al-Mansouri who fled were still gathered on the outskirts of the town on Thursday, waiting for word that it was safe to return.Outrage was mounting on the ground as residents watched the Israeli military demolish homes and set fire to farmland, with many expressing little faith that ongoing negotiations between Lebanese and Israeli officials will secure their safe return.Abu Rached, a resident of Majdal Zoun, said the destruction had gone unanswered by Lebanese officials. “Can’t you see what they did to south Lebanon? They’re destroying it, displacing people – even the [Lebanese] army can’t stay in al-Mansouri,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Trump signs executive orders banning so-called ‘birth tourism’
articles.excerpt: Trump signs executive orders banning so-called ‘birth tourism’NewsFeedUS President Donald Trump signed two executive orders to further limit who is eligible for birthright citizenship – a policy giving any child born in America automatic US citizenship. The US Supreme Court had already blocked his earlier effort in June.Published On 6 Aug 2026

articles.title: Iran’s Ghalibaf accuses Trump of conducting show diplomacy ‘on loop’
articles.excerpt: US president says he is involved in talks and war will end ‘pretty soon’, claiming that Iran cannot ‘go much longer’.Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator has accused Donald Trump of conducting “theatre diplomacy on loop” after the United States president’s repeated claims that he was ordering attacks on Iran, and then calling them off.Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made the remarks in a social media post on Thursday, just days after Trump called off his latest planned strikes, claiming that “the perimeters of a deal” had already been agreed to with Tehran.

articles.title: Was Tarique Rahman’s Youth Outreach More Than an Election Strategy?
articles.excerpt: After 17 years in exile, Tarique Rahman, then acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), returned to Dhaka on December 25, 2025. By then, people’s political aspirations had changed significantly through a mass uprising and political transition following a long period of authoritarian rule. In the aftermath of the July 2024 uprising, Bangladesh’s youth had moved to the center of politics. They not only led the movement that brought down Sheikh Hasina’s government, but also made up a significant portion of the electorate that would choose the next. The youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP) emerged in the political arena; most of its leaders had been at the forefront of the July uprising. Ahead of the national election, Jamaat-e-Islami, in alliance with the NCP and several other Islamist parties, was mounting a political challenge. Rahman and his party did not take long to recognize the reality. After returning home, he placed young people at the center of various programs, policy plans, and the party’s election manifesto. During the election campaign, several events were organized exclusively for the youth. At that time, analysts viewed them as part of the BNP’s strategy to attract young voters. The formal campaign for Bangladesh’s 13th parliamentary election began on January 22 this year. On that day, Rahman was in Sylhet, a city around 250 kilometers from Dhaka. He attended an event titled “The Plan: Youth Policy Talk with Tarique Rahman,” where several hundred students from different educational institutions heard the leader of the country’s largest political party explain his plans for nation-building. The students also shared their views and raised questions. Rahman responded to them and sought their suggestions. A similar event was later held in Chattogram. He also engaged directly with the youth through other programs. The BNP’s election manifesto contained many promises for the youth.

articles.title: How South Korea Can Survive the Unbundling of International Order
articles.excerpt: For most of the post-war era, power, legitimacy, and cooperation reinforced one another. American leadership underwrote security, open markets, and freedom of navigation. Democratic partnerships generated political trust. Universal institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, and the nuclear nonproliferation regime provided common rules and legal legitimacy. Though imperfect, these three pillars generally worked in concert. That alignment has broken down. Security, economic governance, political legitimacy, and practical cooperation are no longer occurring in the same institutions or even among the same groups of states. I call this structural transformation the “unbundling of order.” The result is disalignment, a condition in which power, legitimacy, and cooperation no longer reinforce one another. Analysts today often ask whether the liberal international order is collapsing or which great power will replace the United States. The real question is whether the essential functions of the international order can be reconnected under increasingly fragmented geopolitical conditions. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed the inability of existing institutions like the United Nations to prevent or halt great power aggression. The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran demonstrated that military superiority alone cannot ensure regional stability or the credibility of the global nonproliferation regime. Competition – especially, but not exclusively between China and the United States – over semiconductors, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, and maritime supply chains blurs the traditional boundary between economics and security. Cooperation is increasingly necessary, but the most inclusive institutions are often the least capable of collective action. This paradox has driven the rise of minilateralism.

articles.title: The Rule of Law in Afghanistan Failed Long Before the Taliban’s Triumph
articles.excerpt: Nearly five years after Taliban insurgents toppled the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, calls still ring out for a return to the rule of law. United Nations officials contend that Taliban governance “precipitated the collapse of the rule of law and judicial independence in Afghanistan.” Amnesty International pleads for the Taliban to “reinstate a formal constitutional and legal framework and the rule of law.” The idea that Afghanistan lost the rule of law in 2021 is compelling. It is also a fantasy. The United States, and the international community more broadly, abandoned rule of law in Afghanistan long before the Taliban returned. The U.S.-backed regime that the Taliban defeated was one of the most corrupt states on Earth. And within that regime, police and courts were consistently ranked among the most corrupt parts. For example, a major 2018 survey found “corruption within the local security and justice sector in Afghanistan remains a key driver of insecurity in the country.” The United States’ willingness to not only tolerate but also perpetuate corruption and lawlessness proved essential for the Taliban’s success. What of the U.S. role? Here, too, reality and rhetoric clash. Government officials and outside commentators routinely stress the idea that progress in law and justice was occurring and would have continued. As my recent work in Law & Social Inquiry shows, this is not the case. Trying and Failing At first, the U.S. envisioned the new Islamic Republic of Afghanistan as committed to the rule of law. Yet, initial efforts were outsourced to Italy and achieved little. Worse still, they backed a strong presidency and an unrepresentative parliamentary system that offered a decidedly weak foundation for a state built on the rule of law. As the Taliban insurgency gathered strength in the mid 2000s, Afghan government corruption became a key concern. Courts were expensive, unprofessional, predatory, and generally ineffective.

articles.title: Bangladesh-India Relations Hit Fresh Turbulence
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has said she will return to her country in December this year, almost two and a half years after fleeing to India following violent student protests that culminated in the ouster of her government. In a message delivered online to Indian and foreign journalists in New Delhi on August 5, Hasina said her decision to return home was based on her desire to serve her country and its people. Acknowledging the possibility of imprisonment or even execution if she returned to Bangladesh, Hasina said that such apprehensions would not deter her. “My return, and the return of the Awami League to the democratic process, is not about power. It is about putting Bangladesh back on the right track,” Hasina said. She also defended her government’s action against protesters who she said had destroyed public infrastructure and vandalized monuments associated with Sheikh Mujibur Rehman, who led Bangladesh’s liberation war in 1971 and became independent Bangladesh’s first president. Hasina’s media interaction drew an angry response from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party government, which expressed “outrage” over India allowing the press conference to be organized in Delhi. “Dhaka deeply regrets that in spite of concerns conveyed a priori to the Government of India about the likely ramifications of this event on the reset of our bilateral relations, this public event was permitted to be held,” it said. That it took place on the very day that Bangladesh was observing the second anniversary of Hasina’s ouster was “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution,” it added. On the eve of Hasina’s online interaction with the media, India distanced itself from the Hasina event, saying it had no role in it nor had it endorsed it. The Awami League presser was hosted by the Foreign Correspondents Club of South Asia in New Delhi. But that did not convince Bangladesh.

articles.title: Clashes Erupt at Susta Along India-Nepal Border
articles.excerpt: The long-standing India-Nepal dispute over Susta, one of the most geographically and politically sensitive sections of the Nepal-India border, erupted in violent clashes on August 2 between Nepali villagers and Indian border security personnel. The latter had allegedly crossed into Nepali territory in Nawalparasi West and dismantled an under-construction embankment built by local residents to prevent flooding. Nepal’s Armed Police Force had to intervene to prevent further escalation. According to Nepali media, a similar iincident happened in June, when India’s Border Security Force personnel entered an embankment construction site in Susta Municipality-5 and pressured workers to halt the project, which was part of ongoing efforts to provide protection for flood-prone settlements in the area. India is yet to respond officially to these allegations. India and Nepal share a 1,800-km-long open border. Susta in southern Nepal and the Kalapani-Limpiyadhura-Lipulekh area to Nepal’s west are disputed. With regard to the dispute over Susta, there are no boundary pillars along the 24-km stretch of this region, and India and Nepal rely on natural features such as rivers and trees to mark the boundary. The shifting course of the Gandak (also known as Narayani) river, the midstream of which formed the boundary under the Treaty of Sugauli of 1816, has further complicated the border problem here. Citing official sources from Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Nepali media publication reported that the Nepali Embassy in New Delhi raised Sunday’s clashes at Susta with India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) immediately. India’s position, according to this source, was that since the area where the embankment was built is disputed, the construction violates the “status quo” maintained between the two countries. India’s MEA is yet to issue a comment on this incident.

articles.title: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law is Already Harming Uyghurs
articles.excerpt: China’s new Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress has been in effect for more than one month. Beijing claims the law will foster cohesion and protect the rights of minorities. In reality, it is already doing the opposite. One month in, the law is already harming Uyghurs and other ethnic groups and dissidents. Governments must take decisive action to challenge the law and protect diaspora communities before it is too late. As numerous sources have warned, the new law codifies a dramatic shift away from even the promise of regional autonomy, instead embedding Xi Jinping’s campaign of forced assimilation into nearly every facet of government and public life. In doing so, the law violates China’s own constitution. For Uyghurs, this is not new. In 2017, a Chinese official summarized the government’s strategy toward Uyghurs: “Break their lineage, break their roots, break their connections, and break their origins.” Since then, Chinese authorities have systematically dismantled Uyghur social, cultural, and religious life in what the United States government and numerous national parliaments have formally recognized as genocide and crimes against humanity. The indoctrination Uyghurs faced in internment camps, where authorities sought to replace Islam and Uyghur identity with loyalty to the CCP, is now imposed in daily life across the Uyghur homeland of East Turkestan. What has changed is this: Government actions that could once be described as regional campaigns are now embedded in national legislation. These restrictions will become easier to expand and harder to challenge.

articles.title: Balochistan Is Now Pakistan’s Most Dangerous Province
articles.excerpt: Balochistan witnessed an unprecedented surge in separatist violence in July: 176 terrorist attacks, involving suicide bombings, complex ambushes, coordinated high-profile assaults and drone operations, were reported that month, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal’s open-source database. In total, the attacks killed 438 people, including 127 security personnel. July was the most violent month in Balochistan this year, both in terms of attacks and fatalities. The statistics make Balochistan Pakistan’s most volatile province, surpassing Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where 143 violent incidents caused 244 casualties the same month. The data trendlines of terrorist attacks and killings so far in 2026 also reveal that Balochistan has overtaken Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the most volatile region in the country. As compared to 574 attacks and 1,196 casualties reported in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa between January and July this year, Balochistan witnessed a staggering 765 violent incidents and 1,600 fatalities in the same period. In addition to the increase in the number of terrorist attacks is the geographic expansion of violence to Balochistan’s Pashtun areas, where Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) has been quietly increasing its footprint. The TTP unleashed its firepower on former personnel of the Afghan National Army (ANA), who have been reorganizing and rearming in the province to relaunch the anti-Taliban campaign in Afghanistan. Ironically, ex-ANA factions are using the same residential compounds where once the Taliban’s Quetta shura lived, trained, and launched insurgent campaigns in Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban have tasked the TTP to counter the presence of ex-ANA elements in Balochistan’s Pashtun areas. Recent clashes between the TTP and ex-ANA elements have resulted in casualties among Pashtuns in Balochistan, prompting Pashtun tribes in Balochistan to protest, demanding justice and security from the state.

articles.title: Delhi’s EV Policy Changes the Engine, Not the System
articles.excerpt: At a traffic signal in Delhi, an electric SUV can wait beside an e-rickshaw and a delivery worker on an electric scooter. All three may be counted as evidence of the same green transition, although they embody very different relationships to mobility. The SUV offers private comfort and status; the e-rickshaw provides shared transport; the scooter is often inseparable from a worker’s livelihood. To see only three electric vehicles here is to miss the differences in power and vulnerability. This is what technological optimism does: treats a change in the machine as if it were automatically a transformation of the system. Delhi’s new Electric Vehicles Policy, notified on June 30, and effective from July 1, 2026, is nevertheless a serious intervention. From January 2027, only electric three-wheelers and N1-category light goods vehicles can be newly registered; from April 2028, the mandate extends to new two-wheelers. First-year purchase incentives reach 30,000 Indian rupees for electric two-wheelers, and 50,000 rupees for e-autos. Electric cars priced up to 3 million rupees receive road-tax and registration-fee exemptions, while eligible owners who scrap older cars can receive 100,000 rupees. The policy also supports charging, battery recycling and government electric buses. Unlike India’s national PM E-DRIVE scheme, though, the new policy combines incentives with mandatory deadlines. The policy identified vehicles as contributing 23 percent of Delhi’s winter air pollution and noted that two-wheelers constitute about 67 percent of its vehicle stock. Prioritizing intensively used two- and three-wheelers, goods vehicles, and buses is sensible. EVs eliminate tailpipe exhaust, use energy more efficiently, and generally produce lower lifecycle emissions than comparable petrol or diesel vehicles.

articles.title: Mongolia’s Fuel Crisis Is a Demand Problem, Not Just a Supply One
articles.excerpt: As Mongolians prepare for the back-to-school season while tourists prepare for long road trips, the transportation sector is in limbo. Long lines of cars wait for hours for fuel, sometimes to find no fuel at all. The government was forced to impose restrictions on fuel sales by limiting the maximum amount that can be purchased on select days. The cause of the crisis can be attributed to both external geopolitical factors and internal country dynamics, highlighting Mongolia’s ongoing energy insecurity. The cure might be a path toward transportation electrification. While Mongolia has proven crude oil deposits, the country is solely dependent on imported fuel, with 97 percent of it coming from Russia. The war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East are creating instability in global energy systems, which could impact the supply side. However, despite the popular notion of delays in Russian fuel shipments to Mongolia, sources have not cited any “major” delays from Russia, which makes it harder to pinpoint the cause of the current situation. Internally, urbanization and a mining boom in Mongolia have pushed demand higher, by up to 14 percent annually. For instance, Mongolia imported roughly 500,000 tonnes of petrol and diesel fuel in 2005; however, this number jumped five times higher within 20 years, reaching close to 2.7 million tonnes in 2025. The strategic vulnerability caused by Mongolia’s fuel dependency is a well-established fact within energy security calculus. The government has been pursuing a diversification plan, including talks with Kazakhstan on fuel imports and, more recently, with South Korea. Last week, Mongolian Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources Damdinnyam Gongor was in South Korea, striking deals on petroleum products. The country is expected to receive the first batch of diesel, petroleum, and aviation fuel from South Korea as soon as this month, according to the Government of Mongolia’s social media page.

articles.title: How Kazakhstan Wrote Its Security Service Into the AI Business
articles.excerpt: Securitization of digital infrastructure is not new, nor is the involvement of national security agencies therein. These phenomena have become quite common and don’t surprise anyone, especially as cybersecurity threats become more dangerous and sophisticated following the adoption of AI for hostile purposes. In May 2026, Presidential Decree No. 1258 vested the National Security Committee (KNB) of the Republic of Kazakhstan with additional responsibilities, including in the digital domain. Largely construed as routine modernization efforts, the KNB’s new responsibilities may not have attracted much scrutiny and may have therefore flown under public’s radar, as security agencies worldwide play an increasingly bigger role in cybersecurity. Buried in the bureaucratic language of Decree No. 1258 are three clauses that go well beyond routine oversight. Together, they don’t just make the KNB a “watchdog” over digitalization, but also give it the legal standing to become a direct participant in Kazakhstan’s AI buildout, with the authority to draw private industry into its orbit. Section 14 now enables the KNB to develop, purchase, and operate, among others, digital systems, armament, and equipment and – for these purposes – to sign contracts with state bodies and organizations of the Republic of Kazakhstan regardless of ownership form, with special services, and with organizations of foreign states. In Section 15, Clauses 224-2 and 224-3 vest the KNB with the responsibility to execute the state’s AI policy and the authority to develop and deploy artificial intelligence models and software products. On the surface, these clauses point at data and critical infrastructure protection efforts, and some may even be tempted to attribute these new responsibilities to a growing problem with data leaks in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina’s Remarks Spark Bangladesh’s Boldest Message to India Yet
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh’s latest diplomatic protest against India is significant not simply because of its unusually strong language, but because of what it reveals about how Dhaka wants its post-2024 political reality — and its relationship with New Delhi — to be understood. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs under the Tarique Rahman-led Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government issued the statement on Wednesday night after former prime minister Sheikh Hasina addressed supporters and the media from New Delhi on the second anniversary of the July movement that led to her ouster in August 2024. In her comments, Hasina rejected allegations surrounding the July-August crackdown, defended her government’s actions, criticized Bangladesh’s current leadership, called for the ban on the Awami League to be lifted, and said she planned to return to Bangladesh. Dhaka responded with one of its strongest diplomatic statements against India since the political transition two years ago. It accused New Delhi of allowing Hasina to use Indian soil to launch “venomous vitriol” against Bangladesh, despite prior concerns conveyed to the Indian government about the possible consequences for efforts to reset bilateral ties. The Foreign Ministry described Hasina as an “absconding convicted genocider,” a “convicted mass murderer,” and the head of a “mafia enterprise,” while calling her media appearance “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh” and “a grievous insult to the martyrs” of what it repeatedly referred to as the “July Revolution.” India, for its part, had earlier maintained that the program was organized by a private entity and that the government neither organized nor endorsed the event or the views expressed there. But beyond the diplomatic exchange, the statement itself merits closer attention. A careful reading suggests it marks an important evolution in Bangladesh’s official messaging toward India.

articles.title: US Pacific Command Considers Moving Billions in Planned Infrastructure Out of Micronesia
articles.excerpt: Negotiation failures are leading U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM) to look for alternative locations for the $2 billion Department of Defense investment in infrastructure in Yap, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). On June 29, 2026, Admiral Samuel Paparo, the PACOM commander, wrote to President Wesley Simina of FSM that the country’s demand for a “$1.3 billion compensation package is unreasonable, unanchored to demonstrable costs, and divergent from the spirit of our partnership under the Compact of Free Association.” As a result, “U.S. PACOM intends to move forward by assessing alternative locations across the region to meet the needs of Pacific defense.” Yap state, made up over a hundred islands, is a core part of the Second Island Chain. The main island in Yap state, also called Yap, is just over 500 miles southwest of Guam. The strategic importance of the Yap group of islands was proven toward the end of World War II. After the United States took the region from Japan, one of Yap’s atolls, Ulithi, became the largest and busiest American naval base in the world. Map by Cleo Paskal and Pavak Patel. FSM’s Compact of Free Association With the U.S. In the decades after the war, Yap joined with neighboring island groups to form the independent country of Federated States of Micronesia. FSM then signed a Compact of Free Association (COFA) with the United States that ties the two countries together in profound ways, including the citizens of FSM being allowed to live and work freely in the U.S. Additionally, according to COFA, the “Government of the United States has full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters in or relating to the Federated States of Micronesia.” This goes far beyond usual U.S.

articles.title: As Taiwan’s Drone Budget Debate Drags on, Time Is Running out
articles.excerpt: Taiwan’s government proposed a NT$1.25 trillion (US$40 billion) special defense budget in November 2025 – including its first large-scale procurement of more than 210,000 drones. That was finally passed in May 2026, but with a substantial change: the opposition-led legislature removed all funding for domestically produced drones. In June 2026, the Ministry of National Defense (MND) advanced a NT$210 billion procurement proposal, which led to the introduction of competing bills by each party. The legislature finally completed committee review for the budget on July 27, but there was no agreement. The parties could not reach consensus on any provision in their competing bills, leaving all bills intact for further negotiations. A floor vote could come as early as late August, but if the opposition majority’s version prevails, funding would not pass until early 2027 even under the most optimistic scenario. That means Taiwan could end 2026 without awarding a single new large-scale contract for domestically produced combat drones. This delay exposes the central danger of the prolonged budget review: Taiwan is falling further behind China’s procurement pace and losing ground as its partners accelerate their own acquisition of uncrewed systems. China has reportedly ordered nearly 1 million drones for delivery by 2026; Ukraine plans to produce 7 million this year; the U.S. Army aims to acquire at least 1 million over the next two to three years; and Japan has allocated 277 billion yen (US$1.7 billion) to rapidly expand its drone arsenal. Taiwan’s military, by contrast, holds less than 5,000 drones. A second tranche of 2,032 U.S.-supplied ALTIUS systems has received executive and congressional approval in Washington but remains under contract negotiation, with delivery to Taiwan’s inventory still pending. In an era of drone warfare driven by mass production, testing, and data-enabled software iteration, a one-year procurement gap could prove fatal for Taiwan.

articles.title: India at a Crossroads: Examining Comprehensive National Power and the Road to 2047
articles.excerpt: Turbulence and conflicts have dominated the first six years of the 2020s. Events like the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, and the conflict in West Asia have disrupted the normal way of life across the world. COVID-19 disrupted global supply chains, exposing the vulnerabilities of nations dependent on some others for critical needs. That forced nations to look inwards, focusing on self-sufficiency and self-reliance. The Russia-Ukraine war that followed soon after further exposed key vulnerabilities in global security as well as intertwined issues of trade dependency and connectivity. However, the mother of all disruptions has resulted from the war in Iran, leading to closure of sea traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical choke point through which almost 20 percent of world’s crude oil and other petroleum products transit. The conflict is thus causing an unprecedented global energy crisis. Yet India has been able to wade through these multiple crises successfully and its economy still continues to grow steadily. India developed a COVID-19 vaccine, which it exported to more than 110 countries. India thus won the trust and respect of the world. When the Russia-Ukraine war broke out, it was India’s message that resonated across the globe: “this is not the era of war.” Simultaneously, it withstood pressure from Europe and the United States and continued to buy crude oil from Russia to safeguard its energy security and exercise strategic autonomy. Amid the ongoing war in Iran, India was quick on its feet to secure supplies of crude oil. As a result, India has successfully diversified its import basket and met its crude oil import requirements of 5 million barrels per day in June and July. India is already the world’s fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP. It has one of the world’s largest armed forces, which proved their mettle during Operation Sindoor in May 2025.

articles.title: Malaysia Says It Will Not Deport Rohingya if There Are Risks to Their Safety
articles.excerpt: Malaysia’s government said yesterday that it will not proceed with the planned repatriation of 5,000 Myanmar refugees if their lives are found to be at risk upon their return. Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni announced recently that around 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the immigration detention depot are set to be repatriated as soon as Myanmar is ready to accept them – a fact that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed on July 30. “We have good ​relations with Myanmar. They have now agreed to take 5,000 Rohingya from Malaysia,” Anwar said during a campaign rally in Negeri Sembilan state. Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil told a press briefing yesterday that the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Home Affairs are currently reviewing the plan to identify the 5,000 refugees to be returned to Myanmar, “Malaysia, as ​a responsible country, will not return the 5,000 Myanmar refugees if they would ​either be persecuted or their lives would be threatened,” he said, as per Reuters, adding that there were “several matters” that needed to be discussed with the authorities in Myanmar. “The Prime ⁠Minister has taken note that we cannot send them back if their lives are threatened,” he said. “So there are several matters ​currently being studied by the Foreign Ministry.” The deportation plan follows a recent upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric and public hostility toward Rohingya Muslims, particularly online. In the past few months, prominent public figures have since described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country, while Rohingya refugee schools across the country ​have been forced to close due to harassment and ⁠threats. Late last month, more than 100 refugees were detained by the authorities after gathering outside the UNHCR building in Kuala Lumpur to ​seek assistance, after being evicted from their settlement in Penang state.

articles.title: Artillery-Missile Command: Vietnam’s Answer to the Maritime-Continental Dilemma
articles.excerpt: Vietnam’s military modernization is setting off in a new direction. Instead of procuring naval platforms such as submarines or frigates to defend its South China Sea claims, as it did in the 2010s, the country is looking to upgrade and acquire long-range surface-to-surface and ground-based anti-ship missiles (ASMs) to guard against both continental and maritime threats. A number of recent developments show that this is the case. First, Vietnam established the Artillery-Missile Command based on the Artillery Corps in August of last year. The Command was intended to be leaner, given expanded duties, and equipped with more advanced weaponry. Second, it introduced the domestically produced shore-based ASM system Truong Son and showed off the Scud-B tactical ballistic missiles procured from the Soviet Union in the 1980s, on the 80th anniversary of Vietnam’s founding. Hanoi also revealed that it succeeded in upgrading the range of the Scud-B from 300 to 500 kilometers. In May, Vietnam signed a $629 million BrahMos missile deal with India. Third, it is moving the 380th Missile Brigade from Thai Nguyen province in northern Vietnam to Dak Lak province in the Central Highlands, whose mountainous terrain and position at the center of the Indochinese peninsula can help Vietnam project power further southwest in response to security uncertainty from Cambodia. The 380th Missile Brigade is one of Vietnam’s two ballistic missile brigades, along with the 490th Missile Brigade based in Hai Phong in the northeast. Vietnam’s rationale for this focus on missile forces is rooted in the maritime-continental dilemma. As I argued a few years ago, Vietnam is torn between allocating its resources to the continental west and the maritime east. Land-based platforms such as tanks, artillery, or armored personnel carriers cannot be deployed to defend the country’s outposts in the South China Sea. Frigates, submarines, or patrol boats likewise cannot guard Vietnam’s borders with Laos and Cambodia.

articles.title: Vietnam to Build Memorial to North Korean War Dead Outside Hanoi
articles.excerpt: Vietnam’s government plans to build a memorial to the North Korean soldiers who perished during the Vietnam War, state media announced this week, casting a rare light on the country’s role in the conflict. According to a Reuters report that cited Quan Doi Nhan Dan, a newspaper published by the Ministry of Defense, the memorial project was discussed at a meeting chaired by Deputy Defense Minister Nguyen Truong Thang ​in Hanoi on Monday. Also in attendance was North Korean ​Ambassador Ri Sung Guk. “The ⁠Party, State, people, and People’s Army of Vietnam always cherish and remember the effective assistance of North Korea and the sacrifices of North Korean martyrs in its struggle ​for national independence ​in the ⁠past,” Quan Doi Nhan Dan quoted Thang as saying, according to the news agency. The memorial will be built at an existing ⁠cemetery for North Korean ​“martyrs” in the northern province of Bac Ninh outside Hanoi, the report said. The cemetery contains headstones commemorating 14 North Korean pilots, including two officers, who were sent to support the North Vietnamese air force during its war against the U.S.-backed South Vietnam in the 1960s. The headstones face northeast, in the direction of Korea. The cemetery is also set to be refurbished under the Defense Ministry’s plans. The downed pilots were part of a group of around 100 that North Korea dispatched to North Vietnam to train their Vietnamese counterparts in the mid-1960s. One Vietnamese veteran told VnExpress in 2019 that the pilots were then invited to “fight alongside Vietnamese soldiers.” They flew Soviet-made MiG-17 jets in combat missions ​against U.S. aircraft during the late 1960s, and the 14 North Korean pilots were killed between September 1965 and early 1968, according to a state media report. The airmen were among the estimated 1,000 North Koreans who were secretly sent to North Vietnam between 1966 and 1971. They included mechanics, support personnel, psyops specialists, and engineers.

articles.title: Are India and Indonesia Leaving the Non-Aligned Movement Behind?
articles.excerpt: When Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Jakarta last month, the joint statement issued by India and Indonesia addressed almost every major strategic issue facing Asia. It highlighted the Indo-Pacific, BRICS, ASEAN, maritime security, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, resilient supply chains, and cooperation among the Global South. Yet there was no reference to the Non Aligned Movement (NAM), despite India and Indonesia being among its founding members and the leaders whose cooperation at the 1955 Bandung Conference helped lay its intellectual foundations. The NAM was similarly absent from the joint statement issued during President Prabowo Subianto’s visit to India in January 2025. The disappearance of the NAM offers a window into how two of Asia’s most important middle powers now understand strategic autonomy. Rather than signaling the abandonment of non-alignment, the same principles are increasingly pursued through a different set of institutions, partnerships, and diplomatic priorities. India and Indonesia have long occupied a unique place in the history of postcolonial diplomacy. The Bandung Conference articulated principles of sovereignty, anti-colonialism, peaceful coexistence, and independent foreign policy that later shaped the establishment of the NAM in 1961. During the Cold War, these ideas provided newly independent states with a framework for resisting pressure to align with either Washington or Moscow while asserting a greater voice in international affairs. But the strategic environment that gave rise to non-alignment no longer exists. The central challenge facing Asian middle powers today is not simply avoiding military blocs. It is preserving policy autonomy while navigating an increasingly complex landscape shaped by great power competition, economic interdependence, technological rivalry, and overlapping regional institutions.

articles.title: Has Life in North Korea Changed Since 2013?
articles.excerpt: Last month, as I launched my new book “Witness to North Korea,” conversations with Wall Street Beijing Bureau Chief Jonathan Cheng and NK News’ Alannah Hill brought up one important question: is this memoir of my three years living and working as the United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) still relevant to the North Korea of today? I wrote this book for anyone wishing to understand, as Stimson Center Fellow Frank Aum wrote, “what it actually means to engage with the DPRK – not in the abstract language of policy briefs, but through the granular, often maddening, reality of day-to-day diplomacy and humanitarian work.” This question of continued relevance between what I observed then and the country today is a valid one. After all, I left Pyongyang in 2013 – and yes, things in the country have changed since my departure. Some North Korea experts talk of a rising middle class with cash to spare, of one mobile phone subscriber for every three North Koreans, of ski resorts – all thanks to the phenomena of marketization and monetization changing the up-to-now closed economy and forcing the hand of the North Korean regime to open to international trade. Another thing has changed: data has become even harder to obtain. In 2020, North Korea used the COVID-19 pandemic to deny entry to several EU-member countries that had kept an embassy in Pyongyang and to most of the international community’s assistance programs. These embassies and resident U.N. agencies, as well as most international NGOs, have not yet returned. The U.N. population census remains, to this day, an essential source of quality data about North Korean society. Sadly, there has not been such an exercise since I left 13 years ago. My discussions with U.N. officials and humanitarian organizations point, today, to a continuation of the underlying problems that I describe in my book, which continue to shape the lives of ordinary North Koreans.

articles.title: When the World Stops Fearing the Bomb
articles.excerpt: Terumi Tanaka was 13 when on one fine day the sky above Nagasaki was suddenly flooded with blinding white glare; “a blazing inferno” he would recall years later. At 97 now, he still carries memories of sitting next to the window. His home was hit suddenly by a flash, then thunder, followed by an unbearable silence. Within moments, his city was reduced to ash. “It was literally hell,” he said in his eyewitness account. With the average age of the hibakusha (atomic bombing survivors) reaching 87, there will soon be no one left to provide such first-person testimony. As humanity loses these eyewitnesses — 91,105 left as of March 2026 — we are also losing our moral compass. As the world commemorates the 81st anniversary of the dropping of atomic bombs on Japan, a cruel irony is fast unfolding in front of our eyes. The generation that witnessed the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings is fading away just as the world rediscovers the strategic significance of nuclear weapons — and loses sight of the human suffering such weapons embody. For decades, the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki had imposed an invisible restraint on policymakers. Nuclear weapons were tolerated, but never celebrated. The nuclear taboo — non-possession, non-transfer, and non-use of nuclear weapons — was assumed to be universal and robust. Today, deterrence has displaced disarmament as the dominant concern. Even before the last hibakusha leave this earth, the world is turning its back on their warnings. The Return of the Bomb The nine nuclear-armed states possess 12,241 nuclear warheads, with nearly 9,614 retained in military stockpiles. This is certainly better than 70,300 warheads in 1986 when Russia and the United States possessed more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear bombs. Driven by their detente of 1970s and the end of Cold War from late 1980s, the Soviet-U.S. (and later Russia-U.S.) arms control agreements had really shrunk their arsenals.

articles.title: Why Asia Is More Enthusiastic About AI Than the West
articles.excerpt: The Debate | Society In China, India, much of Southeast Asia, and elsewhere in Asia, the net benefits of AI are perceived by populations to be greater than their drawbacks. Credit: Depositphotos We are living in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). AI dominates the headlines, spreads its influence into all spheres of life, and is increasingly seen as vital to the economic growth and national security of nations. The use of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude have become ubiquitous in daily life. Needless to say, the increased spread of AI — and its impact on relationships, employment, and other facets of society — has provoked trepidation among many. However, surveys consistently show that Asians — and in fact, most non-Western populations — are much more enthusiastic and excited about AI than people from the West. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos in 2025, over 80 percent of respondents from the Southeast Asian countries of Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Singapore said that AI will profoundly change their lives in the next few years. Eighty-four percent of Chinese respondents said that products and services using AI excited them. Likewise, 65 percent of Indians, 67 percent of Turks, and 69 percent of South Koreans felt the same way, compared to 38 percent of Americans, 31 percent of Canadians, 37 percent of the British, and 40 percent of the French. Whilst Japan was an outlier in the Ipsos survey, with 46 percent of Japanese respondents indicating that they were excited about AI, in a separate survey by Pew, only 28 percent of Japanese respondents said that they were more concerned than excited about AI. Similarly, only 26 percent of people from Turkiye, 21 percent from Israel, 19 percent from India, and 16 percent from South Korea felt more concerned than excited about AI. Contrast this with half of Americans responding that they were more concerned than excited about AI.

articles.title: China’s World AI Cooperation Organization Agenda
articles.excerpt: The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Gloria Chen – head of Asia-Pacific geopolitical strategy and business development at Rocky Road Resilience, a U.K.-based specialist risk advisory – is the 520th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.” Analyze China’s agenda behind the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO). The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) was founded in Shanghai this July, with founding members including Russia, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Pakistan, virtually all BRICS members except India, plus a number of other Global South countries, with no major Western democracies among its members. China positions it as an “intergovernmental organization” and claims to aim for the “beneficial, safe, and fair” development of AI. Just as Christian civilization shaped Western culture and ways of thinking, the deeply rooted Confucian culture of China has similarly shaped the Chinese value system and language system. Confucian culture emphasizes moral correctness and face-saving, and is centered on family culture. From the perspective of the Chinese regime, China is very clear about what kind of “correct” language to use to legitimize its actions. Looking at the 2026 World AI Conference (WAIC), China tells you it wants global cooperation, AI regulation and world prosperity. However, the manifestation of family culture is often: “I tell everyone I’m promoting the common good, but what I really want is to make my family prosperous and for me to become a leader.” Because of resource monopolies, long-term wars historically, and internal struggles, Chinese leaders have a deep-seated insecurity. Therefore, they believe that only by seizing power and controlling others can they secure their own safety.

articles.title: Kim Yo Jong Warns Japan Over First Tomahawk Missile Test
articles.excerpt: The Japanese destroyer Chokai fires a Tomahawk missile on July 29, 2026. It was Japan’s first live-fire test of a Tomahawk. Credit: Japanese Ministry of Defense Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, warned on August 5 that Pyongyang would set up additional military options against Japan. The statement followed the first live-fire test of a Tomahawk cruise missile by the Japanese navy. The missile was launched from the Aegis destroyer Chokai in the Pacific Ocean, on July 29. “Japan, a war criminal state, is accelerating its transformation into a war state, taking advantage of the acute and variable trend of the present international situation in which global geopolitical conflicts and inter-camp confrontation are getting fiercer,” Kim said in her statement, which was published by the North’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). She cited the test-firing of the U.S.-supplied Tomahawk missile by Japan, along with Tokyo’s participation in a U.S.-led joint military drill in the Philippines in May. Those moves prove that Japan’s push for preemptive strike capability has entered “the stage of the actual act,” according to Kim. Japan’s pursuit of long-range strike weapons dates to December 2022 when Tokyo revised three key security documents to adopt what it calls “counterstrike capability,” a shift away from its decades-old policy of maintaining a strictly defensive military. The revision, described at the time as Japan’s biggest military buildup since World War II, opened the way for its purchase of 400 Tomahawk missiles from the United States, deliveries of which began this year.

articles.title: 15 Months After Massacre at Pahalgam, Terrorists Target Non-local Civilians Again in Kashmir
articles.excerpt: A year of relative calm in the Kashmir valley was shattered on July 31 when terrorists opened fire on two non-local laborers at a brick kiln in Kilam village of South Kashmir’s Kulgam district. The two laborers were migrants from the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh. The attack at Kulgam has triggered panic among tens of thousands of laborers from India’s poorer northern states, who come to the Kashmir valley every year between March and November to work on construction sites, road projects, brick kilns, and apple orchards. The July 31 killings prompted some of them to return home. The Kulgam attack came close on the heels of the killing of a Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) police constable at a busy market in Anantnag district. The attacks have raised concern over the return of terrorism to the Kashmir valley. Indeed, the incident at Kulgam is the first targeted killing of non-local civilians by terrorists since April 22, 2025, when 26 men, all civilians, were shot dead at Pahalgam; 25 of them were from outside J&K and one was a Kashmiri pony ride operator, who tried to stop the shooting. The massacre at Pahalgam led to India launching Operation Sindoor targeting terrorist camps and infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which culminated in a four-day war between India and Pakistan in May. There had been no attacks on civilians since then; the bloodletting over the past fortnight broke that lull. The killings at Kulgam came days before the seventh anniversary of New Delhi’s abrogation of J&K’s autonomy. It was on August 5, 2019, that the Narendra Modi government announced the revocation of Article 370 and Article 35A – a unilateral action that was hugely unpopular in J&K. India will also be marking its 79th Independence Day on August 15. The run-up to anniversaries of milestone events usually sees an uptick in terror attacks in the Kashmir valley. Since August 2019, over 25 non-local workers have been killed in terror attacks in Kashmir.

articles.title: What a Near-Miss Drone Incident Reveals About South Korea-US Operational Coordination
articles.excerpt: Asia Defense | Security | East Asia South Korea’s army thought they were locked on to a North Korean UAV. It actually belonged to the U.S. Marine Corps. U.S. Marines employ a Stalker VXE30 Unmanned Aerial System during a Combined Arms Live-Fire Exercise at Rodriguez Live-Fire Complex, South Korea, March 5, 2026. Credit: U.S. Marine Corps photo by Cpl. Rodney Frye On July 30, air defense units along South Korea’s front line in Paju, Gyeonggi Province, detected an unidentified aerial track on a thermal observation device (TOD) and local air defense radars. Assessing the object as a potential airborne threat, the South Korean Army Ground Operations Command immediately issued “Durumi,” a high-alert air defense posture triggered in response to suspected enemy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) incursions. For 90 minutes, anti-aircraft gun systems and attack helicopters were placed on emergency standby in a state of high tension. However, the unidentified object was not an infiltrating North Korean drone. It was a Stalker (VXE30) reconnaissance UAV operated by the U.S. Marine Corps, conducting an exercise nearby as part of the Korea Marine Exchange Program (KMEP). While a friendly-fire incident was narrowly averted, the implications are profound. Severe vulnerabilities exist in both asset management and inter-ally command-and-control communication mechanisms along the Korean Peninsula. A closer look at the sequence of events underscores systemic operational flaws. Prior to the exercise, U.S. forces had notified South Korean military counterparts of their flight plans and formally dispatched official documentation. Yet, this critical information stalled at the working level within the South Korean military bureaucracy; it was neither briefed upward to senior command nor disseminated down to frontline units. Remarkably, South Korean Marine Corps personnel were actively participating in the joint exercise alongside their U.S. counterparts.

articles.title: When Small States Practice Buddhist Diplomacy
articles.excerpt: As strategic competition between China and India intensifies, Buddhism has become an increasingly visible instrument of foreign policy. China has positioned itself as a center of Mahayana Buddhist civilization, sponsoring international Buddhist forums, restoring sacred sites, and weaving Buddhist heritage into its Belt and Road Initiative. India, the birthplace of Buddhism, has promoted its own Buddhist heritage by expanding pilgrimage circuits and lending sacred relics abroad. The focus on China and India obscures a quieter, yet equally significant, story. Buddhist diplomacy is being practiced not only by Asia’s largest powers, but also by two of its smallest states: Bhutan and Singapore. The cases of Bhutan and Singapore demonstrate how small states can pursue Buddhist diplomacy under different conditions. Their limited geopolitical weight and lack of great power status have encouraged them to cultivate influence through cultural networks and regional cooperation. Bhutan, the world’s only official Vajrayana Buddhist kingdom, is a small, landlocked Himalayan state that has placed Buddhist values at the heart of both its domestic governance and its engagement with the world. This approach owes much to the vision of the Fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, who developed Gross National Happiness not simply as an alternative measure of development, but as a strategy for reconciling modernization with the preservation of Bhutan’s Buddhist culture and national identity. For a small state situated between India and China, this fusion of Buddhist values and development also served a strategic purpose, turning cultural distinctiveness into a means of safeguarding sovereignty while giving Bhutan an international profile far beyond its size.

articles.title: China’s ‘Internet Addiction’ Schools Are Now Locking Up Adults
articles.excerpt: In March, a 21-year-old music student in Beijing arrived at an apartment complex to teach a piano lesson. Waiting for her were her father, her aunt, and two employees of a private disciplinary institution. Her relatives told her the strangers were police officers investigating a family matter. Instead, they forced her into a vehicle, confiscated her phone, and drove her hundreds of miles to an institution in Henan province, where she spent the next 11 days. According to Southern People Weekly, her parents objected to her romantic relationship and believed their once-obedient daughter had become difficult to manage. They paid the institution to isolate her, monitor her daily life, and pressure her into ending the relationship. Public reporting indicates that this institution charged 26,800 yuan (around $4,000) for six months or 36,800 yuan for a year, including room and board. The incident reflects a broader transformation in an industry once associated almost exclusively with treating so-called “internet addiction.” A July investigation by China Newsweek documented several adults placed in similar institutions by their own families. One 21-year-old man said his parents paid for a facility to “correct” his sleeping habits. A 25-year-old woman living alone reported being taken from Jiangxi to a disciplinary institution in Hubei after relatives and staff entered her home and confiscated her phone. Another investigation by Jiemian News found adults as old as 33 living alongside teenagers in one behavioral correction school. These institutions emerged during the 2000s, amid national anxiety over youth “internet addiction.” Many gained notoriety for military-style discipline and physical punishment before public criticism pushed the industry to rebrand as family education centers, behavioral intervention programs, or youth development organizations.

articles.title: Russia’s New Move in the Kuril Dispute
articles.excerpt: The planned naming of a disputed Kuril island after Richard Sorge is the latest example of Russia strengthening its control over the features. It is part of a decade-long effort by Moscow to use commemoration to reinforce its claim regardless of Tokyo’s protest. On July 28, the Sakhalin branch of the Russian Geographical Society announced the future placement of a plaque for Sorge, a Soviet intelligence officer, on an uninhabited island in the Lesser Kurils. Moscow is expected to rename the island after Sorge soon. The announcement drew attention in Japan given the island’s location and Sorge’s legacy. The island is part of the disputed Southern Kurils, which Japan calls the Northern Territories. The Kuril Islands stretch from Hokkaido to the Kamchatka Peninsula and provide Russia with protected access from the Sea of Okhotsk to the Pacific. Soviet forces occupied the islands in 1945, just before Japan’s surrender ended World War II. Japan still claims the southernmost four features: Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai Islands. More than 80 years later, the dispute remains unresolved. Map of the Northern Territories of Japan (Kuril Islands). Wikimedia Commons. Richard Sorge remains a consequential figure in Japan and Russia. Disguised as a German journalist, Sorge led a successful espionage network for Moscow in Tokyo from 1933 until his arrest in October 1941. A close friendship with German Ambassador Eugen Ott and partnership with Japanese journalist Ozaki Hotsumi gave Sorge unmatched access. Ott’s confidence gave him insights into the German-Japan alliance. Ozaki’s ties to Prime Minister Konoe Fumimaro’s inner circle gave Sorge access to information from the highest levels of the Japanese government. The network layered political information with military activity to validate details, increasing the reliability of their reporting.

articles.title: Germany’s Deportation of an Afghan Without Criminal Record Sets a New Precedent
articles.excerpt: In August 2024, Germany became the first European country to deport Afghan nationals to Afghanistan since the Taliban’s takeover. The deportation process was facilitated by Qatar. This happened after Germany’s “Traffic Light Coalition” government decided to change the rules to deport foreign nationals found guilty of serious crimes, a policy shift motivated by a deadly knife attack on a police officer in Mannheim. At the time, Germany’s then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz said that Germany would not tolerate religious extremists or criminals who exploit the country’s laws protecting refugees. He added, “Such criminals should be deported even if they come from Syria and Afghanistan. Serious criminals and terrorists have no place here. In such cases the security interests of Germany outweigh the perpetrator’s interests in protection.” In the first deportation, 28 Afghan nationals with criminal records were deported to Afghanistan. Since then Germany has expedited its deportation process – and expanded the scope beyond “criminals and terrorists.” Last week, Germany deported an Afghan national without a criminal record for the first time since the Taliban’s return to power in 2021. The Afghan national had attempted to settle in another European country but was found to be illegally living there. He was transferred back to Germany and deported to Afghanistan by plane with 30 other deportees; all of the other deportees had criminal convictions. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that the man had become eligible for deportation after his ⁠asylum claim was denied.

articles.title: How Aging Populations Are Transforming Police Work Across Asia
articles.excerpt: Features | Society | East Asia In East Asia’s graying societies, police are becoming the “catch-all” agency for managing aging, like dementia-related wandering. Credit: Shutterstock About one-third of East Asia’s population is projected to be 60 or older by 2050, making it the world’s fastest-aging region. Public debates about population aging have largely centered on its effects on democratic governance, economic growth, pension sustainability, healthcare, urban planning, and housing policy. Yet one area remains notably underdiscussed: policing. Across graying societies, police are becoming the “catch-all” agency for managing aging as their roles and workloads have expanded in unprecedented ways. Police officers frequently mobilize to search for missing seniors and answer late-night calls from those who are confused or disoriented. As AI-powered scams become increasingly common, officers are playing a growing role as educators and protectors, helping older adults recognize and avoid financial fraud. They are often the first on the scene when older adults experience falls, heart attacks, strokes, or other medical emergencies. They are also on the front lines of social service delivery, responding to mounting cases of elder abuse or neglect and routinely conducting welfare checks as social isolation and kinship erosion damage mental health. Furthermore, increasing traffic incidents involving elderly drivers have prompted the police to engage in driver safety campaigns and to identify and report at-risk older drivers. Beneath this expanding portfolio of aging-related police work lies a revolution in policing and governance more broadly. Silver policing in East Asia is fostering greater intersectoral coordination and shifting the role of the police to that of a facilitator within a broader network.

Après l’évacuation de 220 000 personnes en raison du mégafeu, dont de nombreux touristes, il veut croire à une reprise de l’activité touristique : « La saison n’est pas terminée, mais tout le monde est mobilisé pour qu’elle soit sauvée. » « Evidemment, la quinzaine qu’on a vécue, elle est perdue, mais on peut sauver ce qui peut l’être et tout est fait pour », a-t-il ajouté, appelant les vacanciers à revenir : « Les entreprises du tourisme sont prêtes, les collaborateurs sont là, c’est rouvert, les gens sont prêts à les accueillir. » Alors que les réservations sont remontées à 60 % cette semaine, contre 90 % à 100 % en temps normal, Serge Papin veut rester optimiste : « Soyons optimistes pour la semaine prochaine. » Le ministre mise également sur l’arrière-saison et une campagne destinée à rassurer les touristes, rappelant que « Saint-Emilion, le Médoc, le Libournais, le Sauternes, le bassin d’Arcachon n’ont pas été touchés par les flammes ». articles.title: DR Kongo: Mehr als 4000 Menschen mit Ebola infiziert
articles.excerpt: Zum ersten Mal seit Beginn des aktuellen Ebolaausbruchs haben die bestätigten Fälle in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo die Marke von 4000 Fällen überschritten. Das Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) der Afrikanischen Union gab in seinem jüngsten Bericht bekannt, dass die Gesamtzahl der Infektionen 4053 erreicht habe. Darunter seien 1850 Todesfälle. Die Epidemie gilt als zweitgrößte weltweit und wurde als die sich am schnellsten ausbreitende in der Geschichte beschrieben. Angesichts der gestiegenen Infektionszahlen befürchten Gesundheitsbeamte nun eine Mutation des Virus, berichtete der »Guardian« . Die Gesundheitsbehörde und die Weltgesundheitsorganisation planten, das zu überprüfen. Demnach kündigte die afrikanische Gesundheitsbehörde eine Veränderung ihrer Maßnahmen an. Sie würden künftig Haustürbesuche planen, um nach Patienten zu suchen.Ein Problem ist, dass Behörden immer noch zu wenige Angehörige der Infizierten kennen, um sie vor einer Ansteckung zu schützen. Als Schlüssel des Erfolgs gilt: Wenn mehr als 90 Prozent der Kontakte bekannt sind, sich isolieren und bei ersten Krankheitsanzeichen behandelt werden, kann der Ausbruch unter Kontrolle gebracht werden. Laut CDC-Generaldirektor Jean Kaseya sei die Kontaktverfolgung in der DR Kongo noch unzureichend. Für jeden Ebolapatienten würden nur zehn Kontakte ermittelt werden, während die erwartete Zahl bei etwa 40 liege, so der »Guardian«. Deshalb würden die Maßnahmen der Einsatzteams von der Kontaktverfolgung auf die aktive Fallsuche umgestellt werden, teilte ein CDC-Vertreter mit. Seit mehr als zweieinhalb Monaten hält der Ebolaausbruch in der DR Kongo bereits an. Der Ausbruch konzentriert sich auf die vom Konflikt betroffene Bergbauprovinz Ituri, hat sich aber auf Nord-Kivu, Süd-Kivu, Haut-Uele und Tshopo ausgebreitet. Ebola ist ein virales hämorrhagisches Fieber, das Erbrechen, Durchfall, Organschäden und innere Blutungen verursachen kann.
articles.summary: 自当前埃博拉疫情爆发以来，刚果民主共和国的确诊病例首次超过4000例。非洲联盟的非洲疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）在最新报告中宣布，感染总数已达到4053例，其中1850例死亡。此次疫情被认为是全球第二大疫情，并被称为历史上传播最快的疫情。据《卫报》报道，鉴于感染人数上升，卫生官员现在担心病毒发生变异。卫生当局和世界卫生组织计划对此进行核查。非洲卫生机构宣布将改变其应对措施，未来将计划进行家访以寻找患者。一个问题是，当局仍知道太少感染者亲属，无法保护他们免受感染。成功的关键被认为是：如果超过90%的接触者被识别、隔离并在出现首次症状时得到治疗，疫情就能得到控制。据CDC总干事Jean Kaseya称，刚果（金）的接触追踪仍不足。据《卫报》报道，每名埃博拉患者仅追踪到10名接触者，而预期数字约为40。因此，CDC代表表示，应急团队的应对措施将从接触追踪转向主动病例搜索。刚果（金）的埃博拉疫情已持续超过两个半月。疫情集中在受冲突影响的矿业省伊图里，但已蔓延至北基伍、南基伍、上韦莱和乔波。埃博拉是一种病毒性出血热，可引起呕吐、腹泻、器官损伤和内出血。

articles.title: Schwimm-EM: Isabel Gose holt Gold im Freiwasser-Knockout, Ärger wegen Wasserqualität der Seine
articles.excerpt: Die Olympiadritte Isabel Gose hat sich bei der Rückkehr nach Paris zur Europameisterin gekrönt. Die Staffel-Weltmeisterin schlug im Finale des Knockout-Sprints im Freiwasser in der Seine nach 6:41,0 Minuten als Erste an und sicherte sich Gold vor der Ungarin Bettina Fabian (6:44,1) und der italienischen Vizeweltmeisterin Ginevra Taddeucci (6:44,8). Beim Knockout Sprint werden schnell aufeinanderfolgende Rennen über 1500, 1000 und 500 Meter geschwommen. Nach jeder Runde scheiden Athletinnen aus. Gose siegte in ihrem Heat der ersten Runde und auch im Halbfinale. Für Gose ist es ihr erster Einzel-Titel im Freiwasser.Vor dem Rennen hatte es erneut Probleme mit der Sauberkeit des Wassers der Seine gegeben. Das Training am Vortag war ausgefallen, nachdem der europäische Verband European Aquatics mitgeteilt hatte, dass man Spuren von Kohlenwasserstoffen festgestellt hat, die unter anderem Bestandteil von Erdöl sind.
articles.summary: 奥运季军伊莎贝尔·戈斯在重返巴黎时加冕欧洲冠军。这位世锦赛接力冠军在塞纳河自由泳淘汰赛决赛中以6分41秒0的成绩率先触壁，夺得金牌，领先匈牙利选手贝蒂娜·法比安（6分44秒1）和意大利亚军吉内芙拉·塔德乌奇（6分44秒8）。淘汰赛包括连续进行的1500米、1000米和500米比赛，每轮后淘汰选手。戈斯在首轮预赛和半决赛中均获胜。这是戈斯在自由泳中的首个个人冠军。比赛前，塞纳河水质再次出现问题。前一天训练取消，因为欧洲游泳联合会（European Aquatics）表示检测到碳氢化合物痕迹，该物质是石油的组成部分。

articles.title: Flughafen Leipzig: Nationaler Sicherheitsrat tagt zu Drohnenvorfall in Leipzig
articles.excerpt: Am späten Dienstagabend war auf der südlichen Start-und-Lande-Bahn des Flughafens eine Drohne entdeckt worden . Nach SPIEGEL-Informationen sah ein Busfahrer kurz vor Mitternacht, wie sie auf niedriger Höhe in der Nähe einer ukrainischen Transportmaschine vom Typ Antonow AN-124 schwebte. Mit einem Tritt soll er das Fluggerät zu Boden gedrückt haben. Der Flughafen Leipzig/Halle gilt als eines der wichtigsten europäischen Frachtdrehkreuze. Bundesanwaltschaft ermitteltSpezialisten der Bundespolizei stellten später fest, dass an der Drohne rund ein halbes Kilogramm Sprengstoff befestigt war. Dabei handelte es sich nach Angaben aus Sicherheitskreisen um Semtex, einen Plastiksprengstoff, der sowohl militärisch als auch bei kommerziellen Sprengungen eingesetzt wird. Das ukrainische Luftfahrtunternehmen Antonow ist bereits seit 2006 mit einer Wartungsbasis am Flughafen Leipzig/Halle vertreten. Infolge des russischen Angriffskriegs hat Antonow seine Flotte komplett auf den sächsischen Airport verlegt. Derzeit errichten die Ukrainer dort einen neuen Hangar. Nach SPIEGEL-Informationen werden die Antonow-Maschinen immer wieder auch für Waffentransporte durch die Nato, die Bundeswehr und die Ukraine verwendet.
articles.summary: 莱比锡机场：国家安全委员会就无人机事件召开会议。周二深夜，机场南跑道发现一架无人机。据《明镜》周刊信息，一名巴士司机在午夜前看到一架安东诺夫AN-124乌克兰运输机附近低空盘旋的无人机。据称他用脚将飞行器踩落地面。莱比锡/哈雷机场被视为欧洲最重要的货运枢纽之一。联邦检察院展开调查，联邦警察专家随后查明，无人机上装有约半公斤爆炸物。据安全圈人士透露，这是一种名为Semtex的塑性炸药，既用于军事也用于商业爆破。乌克兰航空公司安东诺夫自2006年起在莱比锡/哈雷机场设有维修基地。由于俄罗斯侵略战争，安东诺夫将其机队完全迁至萨克森州机场。目前乌克兰人正在那里建造新机库。据《明镜》周刊信息，安东诺夫飞机也频频被北约、联邦国防军和乌克兰用于武器运输。

articles.title: Türkei will wohl mit Pakistan und Saudi-Arabien Verteidigungspakt schließen
articles.excerpt: Die Türkei, Saudi-Arabien und Pakistan wollen am Freitag zu einem Dreiergipfel zusammenkommen und dabei nach Informationen der Nachrichtenagentur AFP einen gemeinsamen Verteidigungspakt schließen. Das Treffen des türkischen Präsidenten Recep Tayyip Erdogan mit dem saudi-arabischen Kronprinzen Mohammed bin Salman und dem pakistanischen Regierungschef Shebaz Sharif soll offiziellen Angaben zufolge in Dschiddah stattfinden. Dabei solle der Verteidigungspakt unterschrieben werden, erfuhr die Nachrichtenagentur AFP am Morgen aus saudi-arabischen Militär- und Regierungskreisen.Ein Grund für das Abkommen zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt sind den Angaben zufolge der Irankrieg und seine Auswirkungen auf die Region und die ganze Welt. »Das Vorhaben war schon länger im Gespräch, aber die jüngsten Ereignisse in der Region haben es beschleunigt«, hieß es aus saudi-arabischen Militärkreisen. Auch aus Kreisen der Regierung wurde die geplante Unterzeichnung des Verteidigungsabkommens in Dschiddah bestätigt. Offiziell wurde zunächst nicht mitgeteilt, worum es bei dem Treffen in der Hafenstadt am Roten Meer gehen soll. Es geht auch um die Straße von HormusDer Dreier-Gipfel findet vor dem Hintergrund der Vermittlungsbemühungen im Krieg zwischen den USA und Iran statt. Pakistan versucht, beide Seiten zur Wiederaufnahme ihrer Verhandlungen zu bewegen. Sharif und der pakistanische Armeechef Asim Munir waren bereits am Donnerstag zu Gesprächen nach Saudi-Arabien gereist. Am Abend dann kündigte das türkische Präsidialamt kurzfristig eine Reise Erdoğans nach Saudi-Arabien für Freitag an. Zuletzt verständigten sich Iran und Oman nach iranischen Angaben auf eine Route, über die Schiffe grundsätzlich die weitgehend blockierte Straße von Hormus sicher passieren könnten. Pakistan äußerte die Hoffnung, die Einigung könne auch neue Gespräche zwischen Washington und Teheran ermöglichen.Die für den weltweiten Erdöl- und Erdgashandel wichtige Meerenge ist seit Monaten de facto geschlossen.

articles.title: Punica verschwindet vom Markt
articles.excerpt: Hintergrund dürfte der schleppende Verkauf der Säfte sein. Anfang 2025 hatte die Branchenzeitung bereits berichtet, dass die Punica-Verkäufe unter den Erwartungen geblieben seien. Dabei hatte das positive Medienecho ganz andere Hoffnungen geweckt. Auch die Marktforschungsergebnisse waren laut Columbus Drinks positiv, sodass der Hersteller sogar ein Ziel von 50 Millionen abgesetzten Litern ausgegeben hatte. Im Jahr 2024 waren es aber insgesamt nur eine Million gewesen.Laut »LZ« sind inzwischen nur noch Restbestände von Punica in einzelnen Supermärkten zu finden, danach verschwinde die Marke von der Bildfläche. Zwischenzeitlich konnte man die Säfte bei mehreren Supermarktketten kaufen. Welche Läden jetzt noch Restbestände führen, ist nicht bekannt – Verbraucher müssen also Glück haben. Punica wurde erstmals 1977 verkauft. Der Verkauf erreichte in den Neunzigerjahren eine Hochphase, in dieser Zeit lag der Absatz bei etwa 200 Millionen Litern im Jahr. Später wechselte die Marke mehrmals den Besitzer, bis 2022 schließlich die Herstellung komplett eingestellt wurde.
